trails.bestSeason: May-Oct (Kings Canyon Scenic Byway closes seasonally)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, the Kings Canyon Scenic Byway (Highway 180) that accesses this trailhead closes for winter, typically from mid-November through late April depending on snowpack, so confirm current road status before planning a visit outside summer.
trails.didYouKnow: The meadow sits at the base of towering granite walls including Grand Sentinel and North Dome, among the tallest canyon walls in the Sierra Nevada.

trails.trailTip: Peak snowmelt in late spring makes Mist Falls dramatically fuller but also soaks the canyon-floor trail with heavy spray, so bring a light rain layer even on a sunny day.
trails.didYouKnow: Mist Falls is one of the largest waterfalls in the Sierra Nevada by volume, fed by the South Fork Kings River.

trails.trailTip: This paved loop is accessible in most weather, but Grant Grove sits at higher elevation than the valley floor, so expect snow on the ground in winter months.
trails.didYouKnow: The General Grant Tree was declared the 'Nation's Christmas Tree' in 1926 and is the only living object designated a national shrine.

trails.bestSeason: Jul-Sep (high passes hold snow into early summer)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, this loop requires a Sequoia & Kings Canyon Wilderness Permit — reserved on Recreation.gov during the May 22-September 26, 2026 quota season for a $15 group fee plus $5 per person, or self-issued free outside that window — plus a hard-sided bear canister for every overnight party, with permits picked up in person at the Road's End Permit Station.
trails.didYouKnow: Total mileage and elevation gain vary by a few miles depending on the exact trailhead used, since the loop can be started from Road's End or the Copper Creek/Bubbs Creek approach.

trails.trailTip: This is one of the steepest maintained trails in the park, gaining roughly 500 feet per mile, so start early to avoid the worst afternoon heat on the exposed switchbacks.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail climbs to the historic Lookout Peak fire lookout site, offering one of the best panoramic views of Kings Canyon itself.

trails.trailTip: A short but real climb over open granite slabs — sun protection is worth it since there's little shade on the summit approach.
trails.didYouKnow: The summit gives a rare view across both the Kings Canyon high country and the Sequoia National Forest to the west.

trails.bestSeason: May-Oct (access road may close for winter)
trails.trailTip: The short paved path from the parking area gains just enough elevation for a wide view of the Monarch Divide — a good option if time or mobility is limited.
trails.didYouKnow: On a clear day, the view from Panoramic Point extends to the Sierra Crest, including a distant look at the Black Divide.

trails.trailTip: This is a longer, quieter alternative approach to the same Lookout Peak site as the Don Cecil Trail — carry more water than you think you'll need, since reliable sources are limited along the ridge.
trails.didYouKnow: The former lookout tower atop the peak was used for wildfire detection across the Kings Canyon backcountry for much of the 20th century.

animals.viewingTip: Store all food and scented items in a bear canister or the metal boxes provided at trailheads, and if a bear approaches camp, make noise and hold your ground from a distance rather than running.
animals.didYouKnow: Nearly all of Kings Canyon's bears are black bears, but many have brown or cinnamon-colored coats, which is why coat color alone isn't a reliable way to identify the species.

animals.viewingTip: Watch grazing deer from the trail or meadow boardwalk rather than moving closer for a photo — does with fawns in late spring are especially prone to bolting if approached.
animals.didYouKnow: Mule deer get their name from their large, mule-like ears, which rotate independently to pinpoint sound.

animals.whereToLook: High granite cliffs above the canyon
animals.viewingTip: Watch nesting falcons from a distance with binoculars or a spotting scope rather than climbing toward a cliff ledge — peregrines will abandon a nest site if repeatedly disturbed during spring incubation.
animals.didYouKnow: A diving peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth, reaching speeds over 200 mph.

animals.whereToLook: Granite boulder fields in the high country
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy marmots sunning on boulders from a respectful distance — feeding them, even 'just a little,' makes them aggressive toward the next hiker and can make them sick.
animals.didYouKnow: Yellow-bellied marmots spend up to 80% of their lives hibernating underground.

animals.whereToLook: Talus slopes in the park's alpine zones
animals.viewingTip: Pikas are extremely heat-sensitive, so observe them from the trail rather than climbing into talus fields, which also protects fragile alpine vegetation.
animals.didYouKnow: Pikas don't hibernate — instead they spend summer gathering 'haypiles' of dried vegetation to survive the winter under the snow.

animals.viewingTip: If you encounter a mountain lion, keep a safe distance, do not run, make yourself look large, and give the animal a clear path to leave — never approach for a closer look or photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Mountain lions in the Sierra Nevada can range across territories of 100 square miles or more.

animals.whereToLook: Giant sequoia groves including Grant Grove
animals.viewingTip: Watch these energetic squirrels from a distance in the sequoia groves — never offer food, which is both illegal in the park and unhealthy for the animal.
animals.didYouKnow: Douglas squirrels help giant sequoias reproduce by harvesting and opening cones, releasing seeds onto the forest floor.

animals.bestSeason: Nov-Dec rut; otherwise summer high country
animals.viewingTip: Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep are federally endangered and found only in a handful of remote high-elevation herds — if you spot one, view it through binoculars from well outside its escape terrain and never approach, especially near steep cliffs where a startled sheep could fall.
animals.didYouKnow: Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep declined to fewer than 100 animals by the 1990s before a reintroduction and protection program brought them back from the brink.
